newsitem.title: TURKEY: New secularist government boosts Turkish markets.
newsitem.headline: New secularist government boosts Turkish markets.

text.p: Istanbul shares rose further on Monday amid hopes that a newly-formed secularist coalition would win a confidence vote in parliament in coming weeks, but fell from early highs on profit-taking.

The IMKB National-100 closed at an all-time high of 1,857, up 42 points, or 2.31 percent, from Friday's previous record close of 1,815, but down from a trading record of 1,910 it brushed in the morning. It had soared 10.5 percent last week.

"Market expectations that the secularist alliance would be approved (by President Suleyman Demirel) were fulfilled. Furthermore, there is psychological resistance seen at the index's 2,000 level. So it was normal that profit-taking emerged," said Huseyin Istanbullu from Meksa Securities.
Bond rates fell on Monday by one to 1.4 points, to 98 percent to 101 percent levels, after optimism that the new government would secure a confidence vote in parliament.
Conservative opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz officially became the new prime minister when Demirel approved his cabinet list at midday.
The government's programme is expected to be read in parliament next Monday, to be followed by a two-day debate and a confidence vote after a one-day break.
Yilmaz's left-right alliance is a minority coalition of three parties that is supported by a fourth leftist party.
Overnight money rates remained high at 71.75 percent on average, compared to Friday's 71.84 percent, as banks were squeezed for cash owing to private-sector salary payments.
The Turkish lira eased against the dollar to 148,150 at close, unchanged from the open, but weaker than Friday's close of 147,400.
Turkey's new state minister for the economy, Gunes Taner, said a balanced budget target set by the former Islamist-led government was not realistic and a supplementary budget would soon be needed.
"A supplementary budget will have to come before parliament soon," Taner told reporters during the handover of the state ministry.
"The balanced budget was a wrong decision," said Taner, a former economy minister and free-market champion.
"All problems will be overcome with a fine-tuning within the free-market economy," he said.

Asked about a medium-term stability programme being prepared by the former coalition government between Islamist Necmettin Erbakan and conservative Tansu Ciller, he said: "We will first look at the programme that is being prepared. We may have some contributions, or have a separate work."
He indicated some senior economic bureaucrats might be replaced and said: "We will look into the matter of these changes. We are not political. We will work with whoever is doing his job."

Yilmaz formed the government, still to take a vote of confidence from parliament, with the participation of a leftist and a small conservative party. His government is backed by another leftist party.
